'una lengua que favorece la posición inicial' p.205; rhythmic alternation (18)-(19) and unparsed clitic moras, p.207; §3.1 p.92 *('CVV).CV and p.98 'no es sensible a la cantidad desde la perspectiva de los contrastes fonológicos... parcialmente sensible a la cantidad'; §6.2.2 p.313 tones; §6.2.3 pp.314-315 tone-stress interaction; literature review on word vs phrase stress p.45.
3046.heavy: The author calls the stress system 'parcialmente sensible a la cantidad': bimoraic heavy monosyllables (H) exist, e.g. ('koµoµ) 'serpiente', and the minimal word is bimoraic, but there is no phonemic long/short vowel contrast and no heavy-light contrast within a word ('no existen patrones del tipo pesado-ligero o, viceversa, donde la sílaba pesada sea la tónica: *('CVV).CV', p.92; 'El mixteco se constituye en una lengua que no es sensible a la cantidad desde la perspectiva de los contrastes fonológicos que plantearían la existencia de vocales largas versus cortas. No obstante, tiene un subsistema acentual que es parcialmente sensible a la cantidad puesto que cumple con dos de los tres criterios', p.98). Weight never selects the stress position.
3046.prule: One stress per phonological word, on the first mora (first syllable) of the bimoraic root couplet (the 'palabra mínima'): a single moraic trochee left-aligned to the root (ALL-FT-LEFT undominated). Proclitics/prefixes (nĩ=, si=) and enclitics (=te, =ʃi, =nda, =ɲã) lie outside the foot and are never stressed, so the stressed syllable's position in the full word is set by where the root couplet begins, not by syllable count: ('siβi)=te vs si=('kaβa). Correlates: duration (strongest) and intensity; F0 is the tone correlate.
3046.srule: None within the phonological word (root couplet + clitics, at most four moras): 'sólo hay un pico prosódico por palabra fonológica' (p.313); clitic moras are unfooted, ('siβi)te not ('siβi)('te) (tableau 23, p.209). Secondary stress only in compounds, which are two phonological words: each couplet keeps couplet-initial stress, the second member carries the primary stress and the first member's stress is reduced to secondary (''kuɲũ-'ʃitnũ=ʃi 'mi barbacoa', (''ndutʃi)('nũũ) 'ojo'; ('') = secondary, fn.12 p.55): 'El segundo miembro posee el acento principal reduciendo a acento secundario al que se ubica en el primero' (p.256).

En ese sentido, hay una preferencia por ubicar a la prominencia métrica en la primera mora del pie (Kager, 1999, p. 172). ... Una de las características del sistema acentual es su carácter culminativo, puesto que sólo hay un pico prosódico por palabra fonológica en la lengua. Por otro lado, el acento también es demarcativo ya que el núcleo del pie trocaico moraico siempre tiene lugar en el linde izquierd…

3046.exq_: Los casos de (15a-h) muestra una regularidad evidente: el pie se mantiene dentro de la palabra mínima y el núcleo se alinea al linde izquierdo. ... el núcleo del pie trocaico moraico siempre tiene lugar en el linde izquierdo de la palabra mínima. (pp.205, 313)
3046.tone: Three level tones (bajo, medio, alto), TBU = mora, no phonological contour tones (§6.2.2 p.313). F0 is the correlate of tone, not of stress (§4.1.1 LDA: duration strongest, then intensity). On the tonic syllable the F0 of all three level tones is raised (tone depends on stress, PROMTONEMATCH), unlike Ayutla Mixtec where high tone attracts stress; tone never relocates stress in this variety.

tn.quote: El mixteco hablado en SJX posee tres tonos de nivel: B, M y A ... No se proponen tonos de contorno fonológicos en la lengua ya que no encuentran contrastes que sustenten su carácter fonémico. Asimismo, la propuesta se adhiere a lo planteado por Pike (1948, p. 6) quien asevera que los couplets del mixteco están compuestos de tonos de un solo nivel, tonos de nivel repetidos y contornos no fonémicos que son producto de la yuxtaposición de dos tonos de nivel. Otra característica del sistema tonal del mixteco es el hecho de que su UPT es la mora
tn.translation: The Mixtec spoken in SJX has three level tones: L, M and H ... No phonological contour tones are proposed for the language, since no contrasts are found that would support their phonemic status. Likewise, the proposal follows Pike (1948, p. 6), who states that Mixtec couplets consist of single-level tones, repeated level tones and non-phonemic contours produced by the juxtaposition of two level tones. Another feature of the Mixtec tonal system is that its TBU is the mora

3047.heavy: Syllable types (11.11, p. 293): 'a) light (σ) CV or V; b) heavy (σ) CV: or V:'; glottal stop is a vowel feature, not a coda. Weight enters only the minimal-word / foot templates ('CV.CV), ('CV:) -- it does not condition stress placement, which is root-initial regardless.
3047.prule: One stress per word, on the initial syllable of the ROOT: a single trochaic foot ('CV.CV) or ('CV:) is built over the bimoraic root (11.13). Bare disyllabic roots are stressed initially; a root consisting of one heavy (CV:/V:) syllable is stressed on that syllable; prefixes and other affixes are never stressed and stay outside the foot, so prefix+root words (tʃi-'kutu 'cattle', tʃi-'no: 'spider', nun-'iju 'acacia') carry stress on the root-initial syllable; in root+root compounds only the second root is stressed, on its initial syllable (kene-'kojo 'appear in a rush'; ɗasa-'nu: 'distribute'), the first root receiving no word stress. Acoustic correlates: greater duration and intensity of the root-initial vowel (Ch. 9, Exp. 1). Stress is independent of tone.
3047.srule: None: 'in MXY there is only one stressed syllable per word... there is only primary stress in MXY... only roots may be stressed' (McKendry 2013: 297); stacked prefixes 'are not parsed into binary feet' (p. 254); the first root of a compound 'receives no word stress' (p. 295).

3047.tone: MXY is a tone language (H, M, L on moras, plus floating High tones sponsored by prefixes and by words). 3051.heavy: n/a (quantity-insensitive): 'All syllable types can occur in stressed and unstressed syllables.' Syllable inventory is C(C)V(V) (CV, CCV, CVV, CCVV; onsets obligatory) with no codas ('Onsets are required and codas are prohibited', p. 164).
3051.prule: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the stem, regardless of affixation. In monomorphemic words this is the word-final syllable (32a-f: 1-3 sigma); a prefix leaves stress word-final (33a thi˥-ts͡i˥ʃa˥), but suffixes/enclitics added after the stem (negative -hi, modal -ra, possessive -na, -ʔɛ, -ɲa; 33b-f) never take stress, so stress stays on the stem-final syllable and 'does not shift to the final syllable of the word'. In compounds the last syllable of the compound stem carries primary stress (33f, (11a) tjiu˩ʃĩ˧ts͡ʔua˥-ɲa˦ 'our lips'). quantity-insensitive: 'All syllable types can occur in stressed and unstressed syllables'; cue is intensity with occasional slight lengthening; no vowel reduction or tone loss in unstressed syllables; the only stress-licensed feature is vowel nasalization (nasal vowels restricted to the stressed syllable in monomorphemic words).

3053.heavy: Heavy = bimoraic: CVV, and CVC ('the post-vocalic consonant in a CVC syllable is moraic', p. 94); superheavy = CVVC / CVCC, i.e. a CVV or CVC syllable followed by a stray word-final consonant ('a syllable of the form CVC is also heavy when followed by a stray consonant at the end of the word'). Word-final CVC and CVV are not heavy for stress: 'word-final heavy syllables of the form CVC and CVV do not attract stress' (final mora extrametrical, (87a)). Geminates pattern like any CC cluster (fn. 56).
3053.dflt: Penult or antepenult, whichever is an even number of syllables from the left edge, per the prose of (86d): all-light disyllables initial = penult (máħal 'drought', dáwa 'medicine'), all-light trisyllables initial = antepenult (ʃádara 'tree', zúʕama 'leaders'; also ʔáxadar 'green', jáxabir 'he knows', ʔáʕagal 'Be reasonable!', which fn. 54 p. 93 marks as Shukriiya/Hamar forms). The source gives no all-light word of four or more syllables. Extrapolating the prose of (86d) to a 4-light word gives the penult (and antepenult for 5); the formal algorithm (87), however, would foot only the first two moras after final-mora extrametricality (degenerate feet forbidden; cf. (91b) p. 98, where the third syllable of jáxabir is left unfooted) and End Rule Right would then stress the initial syllable of such a form, so prose and formalism diverge for these hypothetical words and neither prediction is attested.
3053.prule: Right-edge quantity-sensitive (Cairene-type): stress a final superheavy syllable (CVVC / CVCC, i.e. CVV or CVC plus a stray word-final consonant); otherwise a heavy (CVV or CVC) penult; otherwise a heavy antepenult if the final is light; otherwise the penult or antepenult, whichever is an even number of syllables from the preceding heavy syllable or, if there is none, from the left edge of the word. Word-final CVC and CVV do not count as heavy (final mora extrametrical). Formalised as (87): final-mora extrametricality, left-to-right moraic trochees with no degenerate feet, End Rule Right. Stated for all three dialects (UCSA, Shukriiya, Hamar).
3053.srule: Secondary stress on the head of each non-final foot of the same parse that assigns main stress (final-mora extrametricality; left-to-right moraic trochees, no degenerate feet; main stress on the rightmost foot by End Rule Right): with two light syllables before a heavy penult the initial syllable bears secondary stress (ʃìdarátna 'our tree', fùgaráakun 'your poor'); a single light syllable before a heavy one is unfooted and unstressed (ʃidárna, suɣáarkun). Detected through its blocking of phrasal syncope; 'not perceived consistently as such' (fn. 58). Hamid 1984:47-48 argued for secondary stress from similar data (fn. 59).

3057.prule: Stress falls on the final syllable of every word, with no weight or vowel-quality condition (a stressed syllable is pronounced longer and louder, NUSA 56 p.142). Subject prefixes ku-/sia-, the AM clitics mo/si/po and future ya are always unstressed and attach to a neighbouring host to form a 'stress unit' stressed on its final syllable; past ka and invitational ma are unstressed except when followed by an AM clitic, when they are stressed; the negators nó/siong and prohibitive na are always stressed (NUSA 55 pp.175-176). The genitive enclitics =ku/=mu/=tu are pronounced without stress and the host noun keeps its own final-syllable stress (buku=ku, buku=mu, buku=tu with the last syllable of buku underlined as stressed), whereas =kaku, the first-person pronouns kaji/kita/kami and the demonstratives fall within the word-level stress domain of the preceding head noun, so that the stress lands on the group's final syllable (buku=kaku with the last syllable of kaku underlined) (NUSA 56 pp.142-143, 146).

3062.prule: Main accent on the first syllable of the stem (the 'Germanic stress law'): root-initial stress, with the prefixes ge-/be-/ver- unstressed (and in this dialect mostly non-syllabic: gmaxd 'gemacht', blegd 'belegt', frirnad 'verirrt'); in compounds the first member carries the main accent and the second member is secondarily stressed and frequently reduced (medek 'Montag', fäsnad 'Fastnacht', noxbr 'Nachbar').
3062.srule: Only in compounds: the second member of a compound is 'nebentonig' (weaker/secondary-stressed) and often shortened, the first member keeping the main accent (medek 'Montag', fäsnad 'Fastnacht', noxbr 'Nachbar', hédse 'Handschuhe'). Secondary or rhythmic stress in non-compound words: not mentioned (Strohmaier 1930 Part II 'Die Vokale der Nebentonsilben' §§ 52-58, pp. 68-75, read whole; prefixes, suffixes and endings are treated simply as weak syllables).

3063.tone: Corum 1978 sec. 4 'Tone' (pp. 2.21-2.23, frames 32-34, read): siSwati is a tone language with high, low and falling tones ('siSwati does have tones'); tone is left unmarked in the course. Sec. 5 then states the penultimate stress-and-length rule for the word independently of tone. Herman 1996, Prosodic Structure in SiSwati, OSUWPL 48: 31-55 (clean OSU Knowledge Bank copy, read): no stress rule for SiSwati; p. 37 fn. 1 'The penult is longer than other syllables on words in isolation but is not longer on phrase-medial words, implying that it is phrase-level lengthening'; p. 40 'it is the phrase penult which is lengthened and not the word-penult'. 3071.dq: Stress in Tagdal is unpredictable. Most lexical items carry stress on one syllable, almost never on pronominal clitics and other bound morphemes, with some exceptions in cases of the Causative, Passive and Reciprocal prefixes. This section will concentrate primarily on how stress functions in isolated roots.
3071.dloc: Ch. 2 'Phonological structure', sec. 2.5 'Stress', p. 33 (p. 48 of the Leiden full text)
3071.prule: Lexical, unpredictable word stress: each lexical item carries stress on one syllable that is not computable from its shape (minimal-shape contrasts fárka 'donkey' vs bundú 'stick'; báari 'horse' vs hiimí 'clean'; fǝ́lliiwǝs vs affárag), confined to a right-edge three-syllable window: disyllables are penult- or final-stressed; words of three or more syllables are penult- or antepenult-stressed, rarely final, never earlier than the antepenult. Phonetic correlates: higher pitch contour and stronger airstream. No weight conditioning is proposed.
